title: WHO Just Declared an Ebola Emergency — Here's What Every NRI Traveller Needs to Know Before Booking a Flight
excerpt: The Bundibugyo strain spreading through Congo and Uganda has no approved vaccine, no proven treatment, and has already reached two African capitals. India is screening airports. The US is watching closely. And if you're flying through African transit hubs this summer, the calculus just changed.
body:
On Sunday, the World Health Organization did something it has done only a handful of times in its history: it declared the Ebola outbreak spreading through the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern — the agency's highest level of alarm.

For the roughly 4.5 million Indian nationals living in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada, and the millions more who travel internationally through African transit hubs each year, the declaration carries practical implications that go well beyond the headlines.

## Why This Outbreak Is Different

This is not the Ebola you remember from the 2014 West African crisis. That outbreak was caused by the Zaire strain, which eventually produced approved vaccines and antibody treatments after a massive global research effort. The current outbreak involves the Bundibugyo ebolavirus — one of the rarest strains known to infect humans, with only two documented outbreaks in recorded history (Uganda in 2007, eastern Congo in 2012).

The critical problem: there is no approved vaccine and no proven treatment for Bundibugyo. Candidate vaccines from Oxford University and Moderna are under review, but clinical trials have not yet begun. The WHO has described the absence of medical countermeasures as central to its alarm.

As of May 16, health authorities had recorded eight laboratory-confirmed cases, 336 suspected infections, and 87 suspected deaths across Congo's Ituri province. Cases have been confirmed in Uganda's capital Kampala and in Kinshasa, Congo's capital — a city of 20 million people where containment becomes exponentially harder. At least four healthcare workers have died.

## What India Is Doing

India moved quickly after the WHO declaration. Senior officials from the Union Health Ministry, the National Centre for Disease Control, the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, and the Indian Council of Medical Research convened on Monday to review preparedness protocols.

The government's response includes reviewing screening, surveillance, quarantine, and case management procedures at all major international airports and ports. The National Institute of Virology in Pune has been designated as the nodal testing centre, with additional laboratories being activated in phases. Isolation and quarantine facilities at major airports have been identified and placed on standby.

The Health Ministry emphasised that no Ebola case has ever been reported in India — not during the 2014 West African crisis, not during the 2018-2019 Congo outbreak, and not now. India's current risk level remains minimal. But the ministry is not taking chances, particularly given the volume of international air traffic through Indian airports.

## The NRI Travel Calculus

The WHO has explicitly stated it does not recommend travel or trade restrictions, arguing that border closures push movement through unmonitored crossings where surveillance becomes impossible. But several practical considerations should shape NRI travel decisions this summer.

**Direct routes remain unaffected.** Flights between Indian cities and major NRI destinations — New York, London, Toronto, Dubai, Singapore — do not transit through affected regions. There is no reason to cancel or delay these bookings.

**African transit hubs warrant attention.** NRIs flying to or through Addis Ababa, Nairobi, or other East African airports should monitor advisories. Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, and Burundi all share borders with or maintain significant trade links to the affected region. Enhanced screening at these airports is either already in place or imminent.

**Travel insurance matters more than usual.** An outbreak in a transit country can trigger flight cancellations, quarantine orders, and extended stays. Standard travel policies may not cover epidemic-related disruptions. NRIs planning summer travel should review their coverage and consider supplementary medical evacuation insurance.

**India-bound travellers face screening.** Anyone arriving in India from or through affected regions should expect enhanced entry procedures — thermal screening, health declarations, and potentially directed surveillance for 21 days. Compliance is mandatory and the process, while inconvenient, is designed to protect both the traveller and the community.

## What to Watch

The next two to four weeks will determine whether this outbreak follows the pattern of previous Bundibugyo events — contained within a few hundred cases — or escalates into something larger. The WHO's Emergency Committee will convene shortly to issue detailed recommendations.

For NRIs, the immediate risk remains low. But the absence of vaccines, the appearance of cases in two capital cities, and the disruption of global health surveillance infrastructure by recent US aid cuts all point in the same direction: this is a summer to pay closer-than-usual attention to WHO travel advisories before booking that ticket.
